WHAT IT TEACHES — धारिता (capacity): fill a vessel with the SAME small cup over and over, count the cupfuls, and that count IS the capacity. Built across 2–8 cupfuls, which reaches the curriculum row's mastery bar.

HOW IT IS SHAPED — 3 phases. Phase 1 the game teaches by itself and the child only watches. Phase 2 the child does it with support. Phase 3 the child works alone, with a hint ladder that always ends in a reveal so nobody gets stuck. No score, no timer.

FIVE DIFFERENT MINI-GAMES, not one repeated — pour-and-count (the signature one), record-the-number by dragging, pour-to-a-given-capacity, spot-the-unfair-cup, and read-a-measurement in reverse. Four different hand actions across 10 test screens; no single one is more than 60%.
THE MISCONCEPTION IN THE ROW — “children think capacity is only about water” — is designed against, not just noted: the lesson measures पानी, चावल, दूध and रेत, and page 3 says it outright.

✅ FIXED BEFORE YOU SAW IT (self-review pass): three teaching screens named a jug or bowl that was not on screen — reworded so the words match what the child can actually see; the compare screen now names its rows ऊपर बोतल / नीचे जग; two titles shortened to fit one line; and one pick question became a pour-it-yourself question, because the game was running pick-heavy.

❓ FOR YOU TO DECIDE — (1) is धारिता the right Grade 2 classroom word? (2) the fairness question on page 8 is my own invention, not from the curriculum row — please vet it. (3) page 4 is a short bridge off the previous skill; cut it if you would rather go straight to measuring.

TWO THINGS THE KIT WOULD NOT LET ME FIX — (a) every pouring screen shows the SAME jug, because the engine fixes that picture, while SME pathway 2 asked for a differently shaped jug; (b) the pour-it-yourself screens say डालो (informal) on the chip while the whole game is polite आप — also hardcoded in the engine. The engine is read-only in this kit, so both are written up as engine tickets rather than worked around.
